newsitem.title: DUBAI: SOCCER-POLITICAL PROBLEMS COULD DISRUPT ASIAN CUP.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-POLITICAL PROBLEMS COULD DISRUPT ASIAN CUP.

text.p: Holders Japan aim to build on their 1992 triumph and the successful launch of their J-league at the 11th Asian Cup starting on Wednesday.
There is no shortage of talent and experience among the other 11 finalists but political problems could overshadow the soccer.
Previous winners Iran, South Korea and Kuwait and capable outsiders China and the United Arab Emirates boost the line-up for the December 4-21 tournament.

The competition has added significance for Japan and South Korea because both nations co-host the 2002 World Cup. Both sides will be desperate for a good showing on the road to further development of their game.

Saudi Arabia, beaten finalists in Japan four years ago, must also fancy their chances after an impressive showing in the World Cup two years ago, although they have suffered a string of poor results recently.
Kuwait's chances improved when they won a Gulf Arab tournament last month, defeating the UAE in the final.
The record 12 finalists are divided into three groups. The winners and runners-up of each group plus the best two third place finishers qualify for knockout quarter-finals.
Group A includes the UAE, South Korea, Kuwait and debutants Indonesia. None lost in the qualifiers and South Korea scored 17 goals without reply.
The teams will play in the capital Abu Dhabi.
Group B looks the toughest and most intriguing with politics possibly playing a role too -- it includes Saudi Arabia, Iran and Iraq.
Thailand, the group's other team, showed their potential by winning the Tiger Cup in September. Iraq, hit by six-year-old U.N. sanctions, is the least prepared.
Group B matches will be played in Dubai.
Japan, China, Syria and newcomers Uzbekistan make up Group C where the champions and China are expected to dominate. Games will be played in Al Ain emirate.
The Asian Football Confederation, which has steered the championship away from many political confrontations in the past four decades, is hoping Kuwait and Iraq will not face each other.
Kuwait has indicated that it would pull out rather than play its former occupiers.
